summary: 'Chain of proof' is the speaker's own phrase; the established terms are provenance, traceability, attribution and audit trail. Source links help when people open them and when the link is correct, but they can also make a wrong answer more convincing, and they cannot show what was left out. Human review misses many AI errors, yet manual chart abstraction is also error-prone (pooled 6.57%). The evidence supports storing the source text with each value and letting a human verify, with targeted review of uncertain or discordant cases. Standards exist (W3C PROV, FHIR Provenance, ICH E6(R3)), and an HL7 guide for marking AI-derived data is in ballot.

findings.claim: 'Chain of proof' is not an established term in clinical AI; provenance, traceability, attribution (or grounding) and audit trail are.
findings.detail: One targeted search found no source that uses the phrase for AI-derived clinical data. A 2026 framework paper in this area uses data provenance, auditability, traceability and source verification; it is a concept paper without a prototype. 'Chain-of-Verification' (arXiv 2309.11495) is something else: a model checks its own answer by asking itself questions.
findings.source: Fidelis, An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support, Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
findings.talk_use: Introduce 'chain of proof' as the speaker's plain-language label and add once: 'the technical terms are provenance and traceability'.

findings.claim: Doctors who believed that a citation supported a wrong AI answer gave up their own correct answer in 15 of 23 cases; without perceived support they did so in 2 of 25.
findings.detail: DKFZ-led reader study with 46 dermatology physicians and 736 decisions. They answered unaided, then saw the AI answer with its citations, rated the citations and could revise. Accuracy rose from 70.8% to 82.6% overall. Perceived support was not randomised, there was no arm without citations, and the subgroups are small.
findings.number: accuracy 70.8% to 82.6%; kept own correct answer 92.0% (23/25) vs 34.8% (8/23)
findings.quote: the cue that is meant to enable scrutiny can instead substitute for it
findings.source: Chanda et al. (DKFZ), Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance, arXiv 2608.00817
findings.talk_use: Main counter-evidence slide: assistance with sources helped on average, and a source that seemed to fit made wrong answers more convincing.

findings.claim: Across seven LLMs, 50% to 90% of answers to medical questions were not fully supported by the sources they cited, and about 30% of single statements stayed unsupported even with web search (GPT-4o).
findings.detail: 800 questions, about 58,000 statement-source pairs. Doctors confirmed 105 of 110 pairs that the automatic checker had flagged as unsupported. Response-level support for GPT-4o with search was close to 80% on Mayo Clinic questions and around 30% on open Reddit questions. Older models, and the task is open web citation, which differs from extraction from one patient file.
findings.number: 50-90% of responses not fully supported; about 30% of statements for GPT-4o with web search
findings.quote: between 50% and 90% of LLM responses are not fully supported, and sometimes contradicted, by the sources they cite
findings.source: Wu et al., An automated framework for assessing how well LLMs cite relevant medical references, Nature Communications 16:3615
findings.talk_use: Shows that a link is not proof: the link itself must be checked.

findings.claim: In one test up to 57% of citations lacked faithfulness, meaning they were attached afterwards and did not reflect what the model had relied on.
findings.detail: The authors separate citation correctness (the document supports the statement) from faithfulness (the model relied on it). For checking facts in a patient file, correctness is the part a user can verify. Faithfulness matters for claims about how the AI reached its answer.
findings.quote: current attributed answers often lack citation faithfulness (up to 57 percent of the citations)
findings.source: Correctness is not Faithfulness in RAG Attributions, arXiv 2412.18004
findings.talk_use: Q&A: the link shows where a fact stands in the record; it does not show how the model reasoned.

findings.claim: Sources lowered over-reliance on wrong LLM answers, but only 39% of participants ever clicked one.
findings.detail: Preregistered online experiment with 308 participants on factual questions. Agreement with wrong answers fell from 78.2% to 68.2% with sources. 119 of 308 clicked at least once; clickers were more accurate (60.1% vs 49.2%), but clicking was self-selected. Sources were real and mostly accurate, and participants were not clinicians.
findings.number: 119/308 clicked (39%); agreement with wrong answers 78.2% to 68.2%
findings.source: Kim, Vaughan, Liao, Lombrozo, Russakovsky, Fostering Appropriate Reliance on Large Language Models, CHI 2025, arXiv 2502.08554
findings.talk_use: Design point: sources help those who look, so the check must be one click away or already visible.

findings.claim: Clinicians using a chart search tool with a source link for every claim finished tasks 37.6% faster at non-inferior quality.
findings.detail: Duke Health, randomised evaluator-blinded crossover, 20 participants, 7 specialties, 200 cases: 9.67 vs 6.03 minutes. Frustration did not change and participants rated their own performance slightly lower. The comparison is tool versus EHR alone, so the effect of the citations is not isolated; the developing institution evaluated its own tool. In a check of 187 claims, an AI judge called 170 supported (all confirmed) and flagged 17, of which 11 were false alarms; true errors included outdated information.
findings.quote: Each claim made by Scout is accompanied by a citation that links to the original data used to generate the claim.
findings.source: Scout randomised crossover trial, Duke Health, arXiv 2604.26953
findings.talk_use: Best positive example for 'ask the record, get an answer with a link to the source'.

findings.claim: A sentence-level 'click to inspect' interface was rated highly usable in 46 clinician sessions, but nobody measured whether it helps find errors.
findings.detail: Formative test with synthetic charts, System Usability Scale 86.25 of 100. Clicking a summary sentence opens the source note beside it with the matching text highlighted. The links come from embedding-based text similarity. The authors hold equity in the company that built it.
findings.quote: this study cannot determine whether sentence-level provenance improves clinicians’ ability to identify summarization errors or unsupported clinical claims
findings.source: Parambath, Pulpo, Hartman, Sentence-Level Provenance for AI Medical Record Summarization in a Click-to-Inspect Interface, JMIR Human Factors 13:e95644
findings.talk_use: UI pattern to show: side by side, one click, span highlighted; state openly that outcome evidence is missing.

findings.claim: AI-drafted hospital courses with links to their source notes still contained more confabulations than clinician-written ones, also after residents had edited them.
findings.detail: 100 hospital encounters, 10 residents, blinded, 10 minutes to review the chart and 3 minutes to edit. Overall quality did not differ significantly; AI drafts needed less editing and were more complete. Read through the invited commentary; the original Small et al. paper was not read.
findings.number: 3 minutes editing time per course; 32% vs 45% of characters changed
findings.quote: while also containing more confabulations than the clinician HCs
findings.source: Subramanian and Rosner, commentary on Small et al., JAMA Network Open
findings.talk_use: Links plus human review under time pressure did not remove all invented content.

findings.claim: LLM notes from consultation transcripts had 1.47% hallucinated sentences, 44% of them major, and left out 3.45% of the source sentences.
findings.detail: 12,999 clinician-annotated sentences in 450 notes, 18 configurations, English mock primary care consultations. Of the hallucinations 43% were fabrications and 30% wrong negations. The claim of fewer errors than humans refers to rates from earlier literature.
findings.quote: We observed a 1.47% hallucination rate and a 3.45% omission rate.
findings.source: Asgari et al., A framework to assess clinical safety and hallucination rates of LLMs for medical text summarisation, npj Digital Medicine
findings.talk_use: Two error types on one slide: invented and forgotten; a source link can expose only the first.

findings.claim: In routine use at Stanford, AI chart summaries contained on average an estimated 2.33 unsupported claims each (0.73 invented, 1.60 inaccurate).
findings.detail: Automatic LLM-based estimate on 719 summaries from a 10% sample of sessions, September to December 2025. Half of the summaries had at most one. In an earlier sample, errors mostly concerned the order of events, numeric values and wrong attribution. 1,075 trained users; the training video stressed verification.
findings.number: 2.33 unsupported claims per summary; 50% of summaries with 0 or 1
findings.source: ChatEHR deployment report, Stanford, arXiv 2602.00074
findings.talk_use: Real-world figure for Q&A; errors in order and numbers hit timeline use cases directly.

findings.claim: When the AI suggested a wrong mammogram category, even very experienced radiologists were right in only 45.5% of cases, compared with 82.3% when it was correct.
findings.detail: 27 radiologists, 50 mammograms, deliberately wrong AI suggestions in some cases. Inexperienced readers fell from 79.7% to 19.8%, moderately experienced from 81.3% to 24.8%. Reader experiment without clinical consequences.
findings.source: Dratsch et al., Automation Bias in Mammography, Radiology
findings.talk_use: The clearest number for automation bias, from the speaker's own specialty.

findings.claim: Physicians with 20 hours of AI training still scored 14 percentage points lower when ChatGPT advice contained planted errors.
findings.detail: Single-blind randomised trial in Pakistan, 44 physicians, 264 vignette cases, errors in 3 of 6 vignettes; 73.3% vs 84.9% (adjusted difference -14.0, 95% CI -18.9 to -9.1). The control group got error-free advice. Small and based on vignettes.
findings.quote: Physicians demonstrate substantial automation bias when exposed to erroneous LLM recommendations
findings.source: Qazi et al., Automation Bias in LLM-Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy, NEJM AI
findings.talk_use: Training alone does not solve over-reliance.

findings.claim: Showing a benchmark accuracy and a traffic-light rating beside the AI advice raised physicians' scores by 7.6 percentage points.
findings.detail: Follow-up randomised trial, 72 AI-trained physicians, six vignettes, three with errors; 95% CI 1.4 to 13.9, p=0.016. The case rating came from three other LLMs. Same group as the NEJM AI trial, not yet peer reviewed.
findings.source: Qazi et al., Mitigating Automation Bias in Physician-LLM Diagnostic Reasoning Using Behavioral Nudges, medRxiv
findings.talk_use: Interface design can reduce over-reliance: show uncertainty next to the value.

findings.claim: In a simulation with 20 primary care physicians, 13 to 15 of them did not sufficiently address each planted error, and 35% to 45% of faulty AI drafts were sent unedited.
findings.detail: 18 patient messages with AI drafts, four of them with errors. 80% agreed that drafts reduced workload and 75% found them safe. Small cross-sectional simulation.
findings.quote: Each error was insufficiently addressed by 13–15 participants, and 35–45% of erroneous drafts were submitted entirely unedited.
findings.source: Biro et al., Opportunities and risks of AI in patient portal messaging in primary care, npj Digital Medicine
findings.talk_use: 'A human checks it' is a safeguard only if the check really happens.

findings.claim: Making people think before they accept an AI answer reduced over-reliance, and people rated exactly those designs worst.
findings.detail: Online experiment, N=199, three cognitive forcing designs compared with two simple explanation designs and no AI. People with high motivation to think benefited more. Non-medical task.
findings.quote: people assigned the least favorable subjective ratings to the designs that reduced the overreliance the most
findings.source: Bucinca, Malaya, Gajos, To Trust or to Think, arXiv 2102.09692 (2021)
findings.talk_use: Honest trade-off: more checking means more friction and lower satisfaction.

findings.claim: After AI was introduced at four Polish centres, adenoma detection in colonoscopies without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4%.
findings.detail: Retrospective observational study, 1,443 non-AI colonoscopies, three months before and three months after; difference -6.0 points (95% CI -10.5 to -1.6). Other causes are possible in a before-after design. A 2026 Norwegian prospective study reportedly found no change, but I saw it only in secondary posts.
findings.quote: Continuous exposure to AI might reduce the ADR of standard non-AI assisted colonoscopy
findings.source: Budzyn et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology 10:896-903
findings.talk_use: Q&A on losing skills; mention the design limits.

findings.claim: Extraction by an LLM with human verification had 9.0% incorrect items versus 11.0% for human-only extraction and saved a median of 41 minutes per study.
findings.detail: Prospective parallel comparison within six systematic reviews, 63 studies, 9,341 data items, Claude 2.1 to 3.5. Major errors 2.5% vs 2.7%; missed items were the most frequent error in both arms. Sources were published studies, which differ from clinical notes. Preprint read.
findings.quote: Missed data items were the most frequent errors in both approaches.
findings.source: Gartlehner et al., AI-Assisted Data Extraction with a Large Language Model: A Study Within Reviews, medRxiv
findings.talk_use: Evidence for 'AI extracts, human verifies' as a workflow, with a fair human baseline.

findings.claim: Manual abstraction from medical records has a pooled error rate of 6.57%, compared with 0.29% for single and 0.14% for double data entry.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 93 papers published 1978 to 2008, with error rates from 2 to 2,784 per 10,000 fields. The studies are old and error definitions vary widely. Research Square preprint; the journal version was not read.
findings.quote: MRA was associated with both high and highly variable error rates
findings.source: Error Rates of Data Processing Methods in Clinical Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, Research Square rs-2386986
findings.talk_use: The human baseline is not zero: reading and interpreting the chart is the error-prone step, typing is not.

findings.claim: Agreement between two models and a model's own uncertainty can direct human review to the risky cases, but neither is proof.
findings.detail: CT pulmonary embolism reports with Llama-3 70B plus Phi-4 14B: fewer than 4% of single annotations were discordant and more than 75% of reports agreed completely. In coronary CT reports (1,045 patients, arXiv 2611.10502) uncertainty predicted extraction failure (adjusted OR 4.15) but the AUC gain was only +0.06. In breast pathology (arXiv 2502.12183), of 348 human versus GPT-4o disagreements an evaluator sided with GPT-4o in 52.9% and the human in 44.3%.
findings.source: Dual-model concordance for CT pulmonary embolism reports, arXiv 2503.21004
findings.talk_use: Explains 'check the uncertain cases and a random sample of the rest'.

findings.claim: Checking study data against the hospital record (source data verification) is estimated at 25% to 40% of clinical trial costs and 46% of on-site monitoring time.
findings.detail: Scoping review. The 46% and part of the cost range go back to Breslauer 2006, so these are old estimates. No included study measured SDV sensitivity or specificity. A TransCelerate industry analysis (Sheetz 2014, abstract read, doi 10.1177/2168479014554400) concluded that generalised SDV has limited value and supports risk-based monitoring; the scoping review warns against reducing SDV without knowing what it misses.
findings.number: 25-40% of cost; 46% of on-site monitoring time
findings.quote: No study reported the absolute rate of errors, i.e., detected against the gold standard of truth
findings.source: Source data verification (SDV) quality in clinical research: A scoping review, Journal of Clinical and Translational Science
findings.talk_use: Analogy the audience knows: trials already verify data against the source, at high cost.

findings.claim: The current good clinical practice guideline requires attributable, traceable source records and advises against unnecessary copying steps between source and study database.
findings.detail: ICH E6(R3) section 2.12.2, consolidated version of 16 June 2026. Changes must be traceable via an audit trail and must not obscure the original entry. A text search of the PDF found no use of the acronym ALCOA; the guideline spells out the criteria (attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, complete).
findings.quote: Unnecessary transcription steps between the source record and the data acquisition tool should be avoided.
findings.source: ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, consolidated guideline
findings.talk_use: For trial people: AI extraction is a transcription step too, so it needs the link and the audit trail.

findings.claim: W3C and HL7 already define how to record where data came from: PROV (entities, activities, people) and the FHIR Provenance resource.
findings.detail: FHIR R4 Provenance is based on W3C PROV and links a target to agents and source entities with roles such as derivation and quotation; AuditEvent covers usage. FAIR principle R1.2 asks for detailed provenance. 21 CFR 11.10(e) asks for secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails.
findings.quote: Provenance is information about entities, activities, and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing
findings.source: W3C PROV-Overview; HL7 FHIR R4 Provenance (https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/provenance.html)
findings.talk_use: One line: the idea is standardised, so 'chain of proof' is not an invention.

findings.claim: HL7 has a ballot guide for marking AI-derived data: an 'AI asserted' tag (AIAST) plus optional provenance with model, input document and human verifier.
findings.detail: AI Transparency on FHIR, 1.0.0-ballot, page generated December 2025, trial use; no official version at that time. It includes an example in which AI interprets a lab result PDF into FHIR resources. The tag alone does not say whether a human reviewed the output.
findings.quote: AIAST does not indicate if a clinician was involved in the use of the AI, or reviewed the output of the AI.
findings.source: HL7, AI Transparency on FHIR, 1.0.0-ballot
findings.talk_use: Outlook: labels 'extracted by AI' and 'verified by a person' must travel with the data.

findings.claim: Among 13,806 hospital patients in 43 countries, 72.9% preferred that AI and physician diagnose together with the physician deciding, and 70.2% preferred explainable AI even at some loss of accuracy.
findings.detail: COMFORT survey, 74 hospitals, February to November 2023, led from TU Munich, recruited mostly in radiology, nonprobability sample. 57.6% were positive overall. The authors say site differences prevent country comparisons, so there is no Germany figure.
findings.source: Busch et al. (COMFORT consortium), JAMA Network Open
findings.talk_use: Patients ask for human control and explanation.

findings.claim: In a German survey of 616 doctors, 78% saw AI as a huge opportunity and 76% asked for strict regulation; AI use was reported by 18% in hospitals.
findings.detail: Bitkom and Hartmannbund, online, early 2025, not representative. Hospital use had been 9% three years earlier. The press release has no item on explainability or source links.
findings.number: 78% opportunity; 76% strict regulation; 18% use in hospitals
findings.source: Bitkom, KI in Praxis und Kliniken im Einsatz
findings.talk_use: German clinicians are open to AI and want rules at the same time.

caveats: No study was found that isolates the effect of source links on clinicians' detection of errors in patient-record summaries; click-to-inspect says so explicitly and Scout has no citation-free arm.
The key counter-study (CORA) is a preprint; perceived citation support was not randomised and the wrong-advice subgroups have 23 and 25 decisions.
SourceCheckup concerns citation of web sources. Extraction from a closed patient record is a narrower task, so its percentages must not be transferred.
Automation bias studies mostly use vignettes or planted errors, with more errors than routine use would show.
Hallucination figures use different units: per sentence (1.47%) and per summary (2.33 claims). Do not put them on one axis.
SDV cost figures trace partly to Breslauer 2006; present them as old estimates.
The pooled manual abstraction error (6.57%) rests on papers from 1978 to 2008.

Parts of PMC, Nature and Springer were blocked; several findings rest on abstracts (see 'checked'). Findings marked 'page read' came through a summarising fetch tool; re-check quotes before printing them on a slide.
gaps: No German survey found on trust in source links, no Germany-specific COMFORT result, and no 2026 German patient survey (search budget was exhausted).
The 2026 Norwegian colonoscopy study that reportedly found no deskilling (cited in posts as Endoscopy 2026;58(9):1003-1014) was seen only in LinkedIn posts; check before mentioning.
No timing study of human verification with versus without span highlighting in clinical extraction.
No study found that reports the share of cases left for human review under multi-model agreement in routine use.
Vendor systems: Abridge 'Linked Evidence' was not on the product page read; Epic and Dedalus source linking were not checked.
Sheetz 2014 full text (share of data changed by SDV) was not accessible; the often-quoted percentages are therefore omitted.
FDA guidance text on ALCOA was not read.
